specStatements.text: Life cycle assessments (LCAs) are carried out to assess the environmental impact of products in each of these stages:
use and operation during its lifetime
disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

Use of water, resources, energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects is less straightforward and requires value judgements, so LCA is not a purely objective process.
Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be devised to evaluate a product but these can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions, eg in support of claims for advertising purposes.
Students should be able to carry out simple comparative LCAs for shopping bags made from plastic and paper.
The reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces the use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts.

Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials. Much of the energy for the processes comes from limited resources. Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts.
Some products, such as glass bottles, can be reused. Glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products. Other products cannot be reused and so are recycled for a different use.

Metals can be recycled by melting and recasting or reforming into different products. The amount of separation required for recycling depends on the material and the properties required of the final product. For example, some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace to reduce the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore.
Students should be able to evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources, given appropriate information.

concepts.definition: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product in each of four stages: extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

The first LCA stage. It covers obtaining the raw material from the Earth or from living things and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, for example mining an ore and reducing it to the metal, or drilling for crude oil and processing it into a polymer.
The second LCA stage. It covers shaping and assembling the product from the processed material and also the packaging placed around it, including the resources and energy used to make that packaging.

concepts.term: Use and operation during its lifetime
concepts.definition: The third LCA stage. It covers everything consumed while the product is in service, such as electricity, fuel, water or detergent, and any maintenance or replacement parts needed over the product's working life.

concepts.term: Disposal at the end of its useful life
concepts.definition: The fourth LCA stage. It covers what happens to the product when it is no longer used: collection, landfill, incineration or processing for recycling, together with the resources and energy those routes consume.

The movement of materials, parts, products and wastes. It is not a fifth stage of an LCA; it is counted within each of the four stages, so the fuel used to carry ore to a works and the fuel used to carry waste to landfill are both included.
Use of water, resources and energy sources, and the production of some wastes, can be fairly easily quantified because they can be weighed, metered or measured directly and reported as numbers.

A decision about how much weight to give an effect that cannot simply be measured. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires such judgements, which is why an LCA is not a purely objective process and why two assessors can reach different conclusions from the same data.
A shortened life cycle assessment that considers only some stages, or only some impacts, of a product rather than the whole life cycle.

A conclusion chosen before the assessment is carried out. A selective or abbreviated LCA can be misused by picking the stages and impacts that support such a conclusion, for example to back up a claim made for advertising purposes.

An assessment that sets the life cycle impacts of two products side by side, stage by stage, so they can be compared fairly. A simple example is comparing a shopping bag made from plastic with one made from paper.
The total life cycle impact of a product divided by the number of times it is used. Reusing a shopping bag many times spreads the impact of making it over many uses, so the impact per use falls.

concepts.term: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling
concepts.definition: The three actions by end users named in the specification. Together they reduce the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Using less in the first place saves the most, because it avoids all four life cycle stages.

A raw material of which the Earth holds a finite amount, so supplies are used up far faster than they form. Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials, and much of the energy for the processes also comes from limited resources.

concepts.term: Environmental impacts of quarrying and mining
concepts.definition: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth causes impacts such as loss of habitat, dust, noise, spoil heaps and polluted water, alongside the energy used by the machinery and the transport of the material away from the site.
Using a product again for the same or another purpose without reprocessing the material it is made from. A glass bottle that is collected, washed and refilled has been reused.

Processing a used material so that it can be made into something new. Glass bottles that cannot be refilled are crushed and melted to make different glass products; products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use.
Metals are recycled by melting them and then recasting or reforming the metal into different products, which avoids extracting the same mass of metal from its ore.

Sorting scrap into separate metals or materials before it is melted. The amount of separation required depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product, so some uses need carefully sorted scrap and others do not.

concepts.term: Scrap steel in iron and steel making
concepts.definition: Some scrap steel can be added to the iron from a blast furnace. This reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore is mined and less ore has to be reduced.

concepts.term: Evaluating ways of reducing resource use
concepts.definition: Weighing up options such as reducing use, reuse and recycling using the information given: how much of a limited resource and how much energy each option saves, how much waste it avoids, and what it costs or requires in return.

misconceptions.question: Which part of a product's life does an LCA assess?
misconceptions.correct: An LCA assesses all four stages: extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation during its lifetime, and disposal at the end of its useful life.
misconceptions.misconception: An LCA is about how a product is made, so it only looks at the factory.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Manufacture is the stage students picture most easily and the one shown in textbook images. In everyday speech 'production' is also used loosely to mean the whole life of a product.
misconceptions.correction: Manufacturing and packaging is only one of four stages. A product made in a clean factory can still have a large overall impact from extraction, from its use, or from its disposal.

misconceptions.question: Where does transport appear in an LCA?
misconceptions.correct: Transport and distribution are included at each of the four stages.
misconceptions.misconception: Transport is a fifth stage, added on after disposal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification names transport at the end of the fourth bullet, so it looks like another item on the list rather than something counted throughout.
misconceptions.correction: The words 'at each stage' mean transport is counted inside every stage: carrying ore to a works, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to landfill.

misconceptions.question: What does the raw materials stage of an LCA include?
misconceptions.correct: It includes extracting the raw material and all of the processing needed to turn it into a usable material.
misconceptions.misconception: The raw materials stage only counts digging the material out of the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'raw materials' as the material in its natural state and treat everything done to it afterwards as manufacturing.
misconceptions.correction: The stage is 'extracting and processing raw materials'. Refining crude oil, reducing an ore and firing clay all belong to it, and they often use far more energy than the extraction itself.

misconceptions.question: Is packaging assessed in an LCA?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The second stage is manufacturing and packaging, so the resources and energy used to make the packaging are counted.
misconceptions.misconception: Packaging is thrown away straight away, so it is only counted at the disposal stage, or not at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Packaging is not the thing the customer wants, so students do not think of it as part of the product being assessed.
misconceptions.correction: Packaging is named in the second stage. Its raw materials, manufacture, transport and disposal all add to the total impact.

misconceptions.question: Does an electrical appliance have an impact during the use stage?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The electricity, water and other resources it consumes while in service are counted in the use and operation stage.
misconceptions.misconception: Electricity is used in the home rather than in a factory, so it does not count towards the product's environmental impact.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Impacts are pictured as smoke from a chimney. Electricity arrives invisibly at a socket, so the generation behind it is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: For appliances such as washing machines and kettles the use stage often dominates the whole LCA, because the energy is consumed over many years.

misconceptions.question: Does sending a product to landfill create an impact to assess?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Collecting, transporting and burying the waste all use resources and cause impacts, and these are counted in the disposal stage.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a product is thrown away nothing more happens to it, so the disposal stage has nothing to count.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Disposal feels like the end of the story, and landfill is out of sight, so students assume nothing further is used.
misconceptions.correction: Disposal has its own impacts: lorry journeys, land taken up, and substances leaching from the waste. Recycling routes also use energy of their own.

misconceptions.question: Is an LCA a purely objective process?
misconceptions.correct: No. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, so an LCA is not a purely objective process.
misconceptions.misconception: An LCA is a scientific calculation, so it produces one correct number that settles which product is better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Numbers look objective, and students expect a calculation in science to have a single right answer.
misconceptions.correction: Some quantities are measured, but the weight given to different pollutant effects is judged, not measured. Two assessors can weigh the same data differently and reach different conclusions.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities in an LCA are hard to put a number on?
misconceptions.correct: Pollutant effects are hard to quantify; use of water, resources and energy sources, and the production of some wastes, can be quantified fairly easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything in an LCA can be measured in the same way, so the harm done by a pollutant is just another measurement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know pollutant concentrations can be measured, and do not distinguish measuring the amount released from valuing the harm it causes.
misconceptions.correction: The mass of a pollutant can be measured, but deciding how much damage that mass does, and how it compares with a different pollutant, requires a value judgement.

misconceptions.question: What is wrong with a selective or abbreviated LCA used to support an advert?
misconceptions.correct: Leaving out stages or impacts allows the assessment to be shaped towards a conclusion that was decided in advance.
misconceptions.misconception: A shortened LCA is simply less precise; the figures it does give are still a fair overall verdict.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat a shorter study as a rougher version of the same thing, rather than as one whose choice of stages can be biased.
misconceptions.correction: The problem is not precision but selection. If the stages where a product performs badly are omitted, the remaining numbers can be accurate and the conclusion still misleading.

misconceptions.question: Are paper shopping bags always better for the environment than plastic ones?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Paper bags take more energy and water to make and are heavier to transport, so the comparison depends on all stages and on how often each bag is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Paper comes from trees and rots away, so a paper bag must have a smaller impact than a plastic one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Biodegradable and renewable are treated as meaning harmless, and the disposal stage is allowed to decide the whole comparison.
misconceptions.correction: A comparative LCA covers every stage. Paper bags usually lose at the raw materials and manufacturing stages even though they win at disposal.

misconceptions.question: Where does the material for a plastic bag come from?
misconceptions.correct: Most plastics are polymers made from crude oil, which is a limited raw material.
misconceptions.misconception: Plastic bags are made from a renewable source, or plastic must lose to paper at every single stage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Plastic is bad' is a strong everyday message, so students assume it loses every comparison, and the small mass of a plastic bag is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Plastics come from crude oil, but a plastic bag is light and quick to make, so it can use less energy and water at the manufacturing stage than a paper one.

misconceptions.question: Does reusing a bag change the result of a comparative LCA?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The impact of making the bag is spread over every use, so the impact per use falls as the bag is reused.
misconceptions.misconception: The impact is fixed once the bag has been manufactured, so reuse makes no difference to the assessment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the bags item for item rather than per use, because the manufacturing figures are the ones given in the data.
misconceptions.correction: Compare impact per use. A heavier bag reused fifty times can easily beat a light bag that is used once and thrown away.

misconceptions.question: Which saves the most resources: reducing use, reuse, or recycling?
misconceptions.correct: Reducing use saves the most, because a product that is never made needs no extraction, manufacture, transport or disposal.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycling is the best thing an end user can do, so buying more and recycling it afterwards is fine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is the most visible action, with bins and collections, while using less is invisible and is not organised for you.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling still needs collection, transport and reprocessing, all of which use energy. Reduction avoids the impacts altogether, and reuse avoids the reprocessing.

misconceptions.question: Does recycling a material use any energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Collecting, sorting, transporting and reprocessing all use energy, although usually much less than making the material from raw materials.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycling is free of environmental impact, because no new material is taken from the Earth.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is presented as the green option, so students treat its impact as zero rather than as reduced.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling reduces impact; it does not remove it. Melting scrap metal or glass still needs a large amount of energy, much of which comes from limited resources.

misconceptions.question: Are metal ores a limited resource?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Ores are limited raw materials obtained from the Earth, which is one reason why recycling metals matters.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals can be recycled over and over, so the supply of metal is unlimited and ores will not run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is described as endless, and students transfer that idea to the raw material itself.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling slows the rate at which ore is used, but metal is still lost in use and in waste, and any new metal must come from a limited supply of ore.

misconceptions.question: Is crushing and melting glass bottles reuse or recycling?
misconceptions.correct: It is recycling, because the material is reprocessed and made into a different glass product.
misconceptions.misconception: Any glass that gets used again has been reused, whatever is done to it in between.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'reuse' covers anything that is not thrown away, and both routes start at the same bottle bank.
misconceptions.correction: Reuse means the object itself is used again, like a bottle washed and refilled. If the material is melted and reshaped, that is recycling.

misconceptions.question: Must a recycled material be made into the same product again?
misconceptions.correct: No. Products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use, for example glass bottles crushed and melted to make different glass products.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycled glass has to be made into new bottles, and recycled metal into the same object it came from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling logos and adverts show a closed loop leading back to the identical product.
misconceptions.correction: The recycled material is often used for something else, because a different product may need less separation, or less purity, than the original one did.

misconceptions.question: How much separation is needed before scrap is recycled?
misconceptions.correct: It depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product; some uses need carefully sorted scrap and others do not.
misconceptions.misconception: All scrap must be sorted into completely pure separate metals before any of it can be recycled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know mixtures are impure and assume purity is always required, and school recycling stresses careful sorting.
misconceptions.correction: The purity needed is set by the job the metal must do. Scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace needs little separation; metal for an alloy of fixed composition needs much more.

misconceptions.question: Why is scrap steel added to the iron from a blast furnace?
misconceptions.correct: It reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore.
misconceptions.misconception: The scrap steel acts as a fuel in the furnace, or it means that no iron ore is needed at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything else added to a blast furnace, such as coke, is there to react, so students assume the scrap reacts too; and 'reduce the amount' is read as 'remove the need'.
misconceptions.correction: The scrap is melted by the heat of the hot iron and adds to the mass of metal produced. Ore is still used, but less of it for each tonne of steel made.

misconceptions.question: Does quarrying have an environmental impact if the site is landscaped afterwards?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Habitat loss, dust, noise, traffic and the energy used all occur while the quarry is working, whatever is done at the end.
misconceptions.misconception: Restoring a quarry at the end cancels out its environmental impact.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Company photographs of restored sites suggest that the damage has been undone.
misconceptions.correction: Restoration reduces the lasting damage to the landscape, but the impacts during the working life of the quarry, and the loss of the material removed, cannot be undone.

misconceptions.question: What are most plastics produced from?
misconceptions.correct: Most plastics are produced from crude oil, which is a limited raw material.
misconceptions.misconception: Most plastics are made from plants, so they are produced from a renewable resource.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Plant-based and compostable plastics are advertised heavily, and students generalise from those examples.
misconceptions.correction: A few plastics are made from plant material, but the specification treats most plastics as produced from limited raw materials, which is why plastic use is a resource issue.

misconceptions.question: Do the rocks and ores taken by quarrying replace themselves?
misconceptions.correct: No. They form far too slowly to be replaced on any human timescale, so they are limited raw materials.
misconceptions.misconception: Rock and sand are everywhere and keep forming, so quarrying limestone or clay is sustainable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rock cycle is taught as a continuous process, and students do not appreciate the timescale involved.
misconceptions.correction: Rock formation takes millions of years. Limestone, ores and clay are all limited raw materials, and they are being removed far faster than they form.

misconceptions.question: What are the environmental impacts of mining and quarrying?
misconceptions.correct: They include loss of habitat, dust, noise, spoil heaps and polluted water, as well as the energy used and the transport involved.
misconceptions.misconception: The only impact of quarrying is the fuel burned by the machinery.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Environmental impact is often equated with carbon dioxide alone, so effects on land, water and wildlife are overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Extraction damages the local environment directly. The land is dug away, habitats are destroyed, and dust and noise affect the surrounding area as well.

mcqs.stem: A life cycle assessment is carried out on a new electric kettle. Which stages of the kettle's life does the assessment cover?

options.text: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, plus transport as a fifth
options.rationale: Transport is read as another item on the list rather than as something counted within every stage.

options.text: Manufacturing and packaging only, as that is where pollution comes from
options.rationale: A student who pictures an LCA as an assessment of a factory picks the manufacturing stage alone.

options.text: Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacture, use, then disposal
options.rationale: These are the four stages named in the specification, with transport and distribution counted at each of them.

options.text: Extraction, manufacture and use, but not disposal if it is recycled
options.rationale: Recycling is treated as removing the disposal stage rather than as one disposal route with impacts of its own.

mcqs.stem: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?

options.text: To assess the environmental impact of it across its whole life
options.rationale: This is the purpose given in the specification: to assess environmental impact in each of the four stages.

options.text: To find the profit the product will make once it goes on sale
options.rationale: The word 'assessment' is read as a business appraisal rather than an environmental one.

options.text: To measure the pollution given off by the factory that makes it
options.rationale: Reduces the LCA to the manufacturing stage, the stage students picture first.

options.text: To produce one objective score that ranks it against rivals
options.rationale: Treats the LCA as a purely objective calculation with a single right answer.

mcqs.stem: An LCA is carried out on a poly(ethene) shopping bag. Which of these is counted in the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage?

options.text: Only the drilling for crude oil, and not the refining that follows it
options.rationale: 'Raw materials' is read as the material in its natural state, so the processing is pushed into manufacturing.

options.text: Growing and harvesting the plants that most plastics are made from
options.rationale: Assumes most plastics come from plant material rather than from crude oil.

options.text: Blowing molten polymer into a thin film to form the bag
options.rationale: Shaping the polymer into the finished bag belongs to the manufacturing and packaging stage.

options.text: Drilling for crude oil and processing it into poly(ethene)
options.rationale: The stage is 'extracting and processing raw materials', so the drilling and the processing into the polymer both belong to it.

mcqs.stem: An LCA is carried out on a jar of jam sold in a glass jar. Which of these belongs to the 'manufacturing and packaging' stage?

options.text: Only the work done inside the factory, as transport is its own stage
options.rationale: Transport is treated as a separate stage instead of being counted within each stage.

options.text: Moulding the hot glass and boxing the jars for delivery
options.rationale: Shaping the product, and making and filling its packaging, are exactly what this stage covers.

options.text: The cardboard tray is left out, as it is not part of the product
options.rationale: Packaging is dismissed because it is not the item the customer wants, although it is named in this stage.

options.text: Quarrying the limestone and sand that the glass is made from
options.rationale: Quarrying belongs to the extracting and processing raw materials stage, not to manufacturing.

mcqs.stem: Two washing machines have the same impacts at every stage but one: machine A uses less electricity and less water per wash. Which stage of the LCA does this difference belong to?

options.text: Use and operation during its lifetime, as less energy and water are used
options.rationale: Resources consumed while the machine is in service are counted in the third stage of the LCA.

options.text: No stage at all, since electricity is used at home and not at a works
options.rationale: Electricity arriving at a socket is treated as having no impact behind it.

options.text: Manufacturing and packaging, since the factory sets how efficient it is
options.rationale: Every difference is pushed back to the factory, the stage students think of first.

options.text: Disposal at the end of its useful life, as it will last a long time
options.rationale: Confuses efficiency in use with durability, which affects when disposal happens, not this difference.

mcqs.stem: In an LCA of tinned food, where is the impact of the lorry journeys that carry the tins to the shops counted?

options.text: In a separate transport stage, added on after the four main stages
options.rationale: The mention of transport at the end of the list is read as a fifth stage.

options.text: In manufacturing and packaging, as the factory arranges delivery
options.rationale: Anything organised by the manufacturer is assumed to sit in the manufacturing stage.

options.text: Nowhere, because the lorries belong to a delivery firm
options.rationale: Ownership is treated as deciding whether an impact belongs in the assessment.

options.text: Within each stage, since transport is included at all four stages
options.rationale: The specification includes transport and distribution at each stage, not as a stage of its own.

mcqs.stem: A plastic garden chair is collected and buried in landfill at the end of its life. Which statement about the disposal stage of its LCA is correct?

options.text: Nothing is counted, because a chair sent to landfill is not processed
options.rationale: Landfill is treated as the end of the story, with no further resources used.

options.text: The transport of the chair and the burying of it are counted
options.rationale: Disposal includes collection and transport as well as the landfill itself, since transport is counted at each stage.

options.text: Only the burying counts, since the lorry journey is a separate stage
options.rationale: Transport is separated out instead of being counted within the disposal stage.

options.text: Only the land the chair takes up in the landfill is counted
options.rationale: Picks the most visible feature of landfill and ignores the resources used to get the waste there.

mcqs.stem: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?

options.text: The harm a pollutant does to a nearby river
options.rationale: Valuing harm is confused with measuring the amount of pollutant released.

options.text: How strongly local people object to the works
options.rationale: Treats every part of an LCA as something an objective number can be put on.

options.text: The mass of water used to make the item
options.rationale: Use of water is named in the specification as something that can be quantified fairly easily.

options.text: The worth of the wildlife lost near a mine
options.rationale: Placing a value on lost wildlife is a value judgement, not a measurement.

mcqs.stem: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?

options.text: Because different scientists measure the energy used in different units
options.rationale: Blames a clerical problem that converting units would fix, rather than the judgements involved.

options.text: Because the mass of waste made can never be measured accurately
options.rationale: Production of some wastes is named by the specification as fairly easily quantified.

options.text: Because the firm that pays for it picks the better product
options.rationale: Confuses deliberate misuse of a selective LCA with the value judgements inherent in any LCA.

options.text: Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives for an LCA not being a purely objective process.

mcqs.stem: Two teams carry out a full LCA on the same paint and reach opposite conclusions, although both used the same measured data for water, energy and waste. What is the best explanation?

options.text: One of the two teams must have made an arithmetic error somewhere
options.rationale: Assumes an LCA is a calculation with one right answer, so any disagreement must be an error.

options.text: The teams gave the pollutant effects of this paint different weights
options.rationale: Allocating values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, so the same data can support different conclusions.

options.text: Pollutant effects cannot go into an LCA at all, so both teams guessed
options.rationale: Overcorrects: pollutant effects are included, but allocating values to them is less straightforward.

options.text: Data on water and energy use is unreliable and varies by team
options.rationale: Contradicts the stem and the specification, which says such use can be quantified fairly easily.

mcqs.stem: What is the main risk of using a selective or abbreviated LCA?

options.text: It gives less accurate figures, as fewer decimal places are used
options.rationale: Treats an abbreviated LCA as a rougher version of the same study rather than a biased selection.

options.text: It removes all of the value judgements from the assessment
options.rationale: Shortening the study does not turn it into a purely objective process.

options.text: It can be used to support a conclusion decided beforehand
options.rationale: The specification warns that selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.

options.text: It takes much longer to carry out than a full study
options.rationale: Reverses the obvious feature of an abbreviated assessment, which is that it is quicker.

mcqs.stem: An advert calls a new drinks carton 'the greenest on the market', citing an LCA that assessed only the manufacturing stage. Which criticism of the claim is valid?

options.text: Stages that favour rival cartons have been left out
options.rationale: A selective LCA that omits extraction, use and disposal can be shaped to support a pre-determined conclusion.

options.text: Advertising claims can never be based on data from an LCA
options.rationale: Rejects the source outright instead of identifying the stages that were left out.

options.text: Manufacturing impacts cannot be quantified in a reliable way
options.rationale: Energy, water and waste at the manufacturing stage are among the easier quantities to measure.

options.text: Manufacturing is the only stage an LCA is able to assess
options.rationale: Restates the factory-only view of an LCA rather than criticising the advert.

mcqs.stem: A comparative LCA of a plastic bag and a paper bag shows that the paper bag needs more energy and more water to make. A student concludes that paper bags are worse for the environment. Why is that conclusion unsafe?

options.text: Paper comes from trees, so a paper bag can have no impact at all
options.rationale: Renewable is taken to mean harmless, so the manufacturing figures are dismissed.

options.text: The remaining stages, including reuse and disposal, have not been considered
options.rationale: A comparative LCA must cover all four stages before either bag can be judged overall.

options.text: Energy and water use cannot be quantified, so the figures mean little
options.rationale: Contradicts the specification, which names these as fairly easily quantified.

options.text: A comparative LCA can only compare products made from one material
options.rationale: Invents a restriction; comparing different materials is exactly what this LCA is for.

mcqs.stem: In a comparative LCA of shopping bags, which factor has the greatest effect on the environmental impact per use of a bag?

options.text: Nothing after manufacture, as the impact is fixed at the factory
options.rationale: Compares the bags item for item instead of per use, so reuse is ignored.

options.text: Whether the material will break down in a landfill site
options.rationale: Lets the disposal stage decide the whole comparison, which is the usual bias against plastic.

options.text: The number of times the bag is reused before it is thrown out
options.rationale: The impact of making the bag is divided by the number of uses, so reuse lowers the impact per use.

options.text: The colour of the printing ink used on the outside
options.rationale: Picks a visible but trivial difference rather than one that changes resource or energy use.

mcqs.stem: In a simple comparative LCA, why can a paper shopping bag have a greater impact than a plastic one at the raw materials and manufacturing stages?

options.text: More energy and water are needed to turn the wood into paper
options.rationale: Pulping and drying are energy and water intensive, and a paper bag needs far more material by mass.

options.text: Paper rots away, and biodegradable materials cost more to manufacture
options.rationale: Attaches the disposal property of paper to the manufacturing stage, where it does not apply.

options.text: Plastic bags come from a renewable source, but paper bags do not
options.rationale: Reverses the sources: most plastics come from crude oil, a limited raw material.

options.text: Paper bags are heavier, so they take longer to rot down
options.rationale: Mixes a true fact about mass with a claim about disposal that does not affect these two stages.

mcqs.stem: Which action by an end user reduces the use of limited resources by the greatest amount?

options.text: Recycling each product carefully after using it once
options.rationale: Ranks recycling above reduction because it is the most visible green action.

options.text: Choosing products whose packaging can be recycled
options.rationale: Assumes recyclable packaging carries no impact of its own, ignoring the reprocessing energy.

options.text: Sending the waste to be burned instead of buried
options.rationale: Changes the disposal route without reducing the raw materials used in the first place.

options.text: Buying fewer new products in the first place
options.rationale: Reduction in use avoids extraction, manufacture, transport and disposal altogether, so it saves the most.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium drinks cans are collected and recycled instead of being replaced by new aluminium extracted from its ore. Which statement about this is correct?

options.text: Recycling the cans needs no energy at all, unlike extraction
options.rationale: Treats recycling as impact free, when melting and reprocessing still use large amounts of energy.

options.text: Aluminium ore becomes renewable once the cans are recycled
options.rationale: Endless recycling is transferred to the ore itself, which remains a limited raw material.

options.text: Less ore has to be mined and far less energy is needed overall
options.rationale: Recycling reduces both the use of a limited raw material and the energy needed to obtain the metal.

options.text: The recycled aluminium is purer than metal made from ore
options.rationale: Recycled metal usually contains more impurities, since scrap is mixed; purity is not the benefit.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the raw materials used to make metals, glass, clay ceramics and most plastics is correct?

options.text: Most plastics are made from plants, so they are a renewable source
options.rationale: Generalises from plant-based plastics, although most plastics come from crude oil.

options.text: They are unlimited, because these products can be recycled
options.rationale: Confuses the ability to recycle a material with an unlimited supply of the raw material.

options.text: Only metals are limited; glass and clay are unlimited
options.rationale: Sand and clay feel abundant, so their supply is assumed to be endless.

options.text: They all come from limited raw materials found in the Earth
options.rationale: The specification states that all of these are produced from limited raw materials.

mcqs.stem: A company quarries limestone to make cement. Which of these is the best description of the environmental impact of the quarrying?

options.text: Dust, noise and the loss of habitat around the quarry site
options.rationale: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying causes exactly these local environmental impacts.

options.text: There is no lasting impact, as the site will be landscaped later
options.rationale: Restoration at the end is treated as cancelling the impacts of the working quarry.

options.text: The only impact is the fuel burned by the machines there
options.rationale: Environmental impact is equated with carbon dioxide alone, ignoring land, water and habitat.

options.text: None, as limestone re-forms quickly and can be quarried again
options.rationale: The rock cycle is assumed to work on a human timescale, so quarrying is judged harmless.

mcqs.stem: A glass bottle is returned to the dairy, washed and then filled with milk again. Which term describes what has happened to the bottle, and why?

options.text: Recycling, because the glass has been used for a second time
options.rationale: Any second use of a material is labelled recycling, whatever happened in between.

options.text: Reuse, because the bottle is used again as it is
options.rationale: The object itself is used again without the material being reprocessed, which is reuse.

options.text: Reduction, because fewer new bottles now need making
options.rationale: Confuses an outcome of reuse with reduction in the amount of product used.

options.text: Recycling, since the bottle was collected for processing
options.rationale: Collection schemes are associated with recycling, so washing is read as reprocessing.

mcqs.stem: Waste glass bottles are crushed and melted, and the glass is then made into new glass jars. Why is this recycling rather than reuse?

options.text: The glass has been reprocessed and made into a different product
options.rationale: Crushing and melting reprocesses the material, so the bottles have been recycled, not reused.

options.text: It is reuse, because the same glass is being used once more
options.rationale: Uses the everyday meaning of reuse, in which anything not thrown away counts.

options.text: Recycled glass must always be turned back into bottles
options.rationale: Assumes a closed loop to the identical product, although the specification describes different glass products.

options.text: It is reduction, because fewer new jars have to be made
options.rationale: Applies the label reduction to a saving that comes from recycling the material.

mcqs.stem: How are metals recycled?

options.text: They are dissolved in acid, and the metal is then filtered out
options.rationale: Imports a laboratory separation method that would be impractical and energy costly on this scale.

options.text: They are melted and then recast or reformed into products
options.rationale: This is the method given in the specification for recycling metals.

options.text: They are melted only when every metal has been separated
options.rationale: Assumes complete purity is always needed, although the separation required depends on the final use.

options.text: They are crushed to powder and pressed into new shapes
options.rationale: Transfers a process used for some other materials to metals, which are melted instead.

mcqs.stem: At a steelworks, some scrap steel is added to the molten iron that comes from a blast furnace. Why is this done?

options.text: It acts as a fuel in the furnace, so less coke has to be burned
options.rationale: Everything else added to a blast furnace reacts, so the scrap is assumed to react as well.

options.text: It removes the need to use any iron ore at the works at all
options.rationale: 'Reduce the amount' is read as 'remove the need', which the specification does not say.

options.text: It separates unwanted metals out of the molten iron
options.rationale: Adding scrap is confused with purification, since separation is linked to recycling in students' minds.

options.text: It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from ore
options.rationale: This is the reason given in the specification: less iron then has to be extracted from iron ore.

mcqs.stem: A council has data on four schemes. New raw material avoided each year: repair scheme 900 t, kerbside recycling 400 t, recycled bin bags 120 t, burning waste 0 t. Which scheme cuts the use of limited resources the most?

options.text: Kerbside recycling of bottles and cans
options.rationale: Recycling is the most visible action, so it is picked although the data gives it only 400 t.

options.text: A repair scheme for household goods
options.rationale: The data gives the repair scheme 900 t, the largest saving of new raw material.

options.text: Bin bags made from recycled waste
options.rationale: Recycled content is treated as impact free, but the data gives this scheme only 120 t.

options.text: Burning waste to generate electricity
options.rationale: Changes how the waste is disposed of; the data shows it avoids no new raw material.

mcqs.stem: A plastic bag needs 0.6 MJ to make and is used once. A paper bag needs 2.0 MJ to make and is reused 4 times. What is the energy used per use of the paper bag?

options.text: 0.5 MJ
options.rationale: Impact per use is the total divided by the number of uses: 2.0 MJ divided by 4 is 0.5 MJ.

options.text: 2.0 MJ
options.rationale: Treats the impact as fixed once the bag is made, so the figure is never divided by the uses.

options.text: 8.0 MJ
options.rationale: Multiplies 2.0 MJ by the 4 uses instead of dividing, which gives the energy for four new bags.

options.text: 1.4 MJ
options.rationale: Subtracts the plastic figure from the paper one, which compares the bags but is not a per use value.

mcqs.stem: A comparative LCA gives the energy to make each bag: paper 2.0 MJ, plastic 0.6 MJ. A shopper reuses a paper bag 10 times and uses a plastic bag once. Which conclusion do these figures support?

options.text: Per use the paper bag uses less energy than the plastic bag
options.rationale: 2.0 MJ shared over 10 uses is 0.2 MJ per use, which is below the plastic bag's 0.6 MJ.

options.text: The plastic bag uses less energy per use than the paper
options.rationale: Compares the bags item for item, so the 10 uses of the paper bag are left out of the sum.

options.text: Energy use cannot be quantified, so the figures prove nothing
options.rationale: Energy use is named in the specification as something quantified fairly easily.

options.text: Plastic comes from a renewable source, so plastic wins
options.rationale: Most plastics come from crude oil, a limited raw material, and this ignores the figures.
